questions.q: 'You ___ submit the form by Friday — it is compulsory.'
questions.a: 'must' — 'compulsory' makes it obligation, not advice. A wrong answer 'should' understates a requirement as a suggestion — the strength-mismatch error.

questions.q: '___ I use your phone?' — formal permission to a teacher.
questions.a: 'May' — the formal permission modal. 'Can' is grammatical but casual; boards prefer 'may' when register is tested. A wrong answer 'must' changes the function to obligation.

questions.q: 'It ___ rain tonight — dark clouds are gathering.' may or will?
questions.a: 'may' — clouds suggest possibility, not certainty; 'will' would claim the forecast is settled. A wrong answer 'will' shows the student reads modals as tense markers, not strength markers.

questions.q: Modals are graded on function: ability (can/could), permission (may/can), obligation (must), advice (should/ought to), ______ (may/might/could), request (would/could).
Fill in the blank: Modals are graded on function: ability (can/could), permission (may/can), obligation (must), advice (should/ought to), ______ (may/might/could), request (would/could).
Fill in the blank: The ______ ladder: might < may < could < will(probability).
What is Modals? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Modals are graded on function: ability (can/could), permission (may/can), obligation (must), advice (should/ought to), possibility (may/might/could), request (would/could).

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Modals?
questions.a: Students pick by politeness-feel, overusing 'should' and 'can', and treat 'must'/'should' as synonyms — the strength distinction is invisible to them.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student selects the modal matching the context's function and strength, distinguishes must/should obligation levels and may/might possibility levels, and uses the formal-permission 'may' correctly.
